9160:
To tolerate something means to put up with it — to endure it, even if you dislike it. You grit your teeth and bear it.

Intolerable is the opposite. The prefix "in-" flips the meaning entirely, just like "invisible" means "not visible" or "incomplete" means "not complete."

So, intolerable means:

So bad, painful, or unacceptable that a person simply cannot endure it anymore.

It describes a situation, feeling, behavior, or condition that has gone far beyond what any reasonable person can be expected to put up with. It signals that a limit has been crossed — a breaking point.

Think of tolerance as a cup. Unpleasant things fill that cup. Most difficulties — a noisy neighbor, a boring meeting, mild discomfort — fill the cup partially. You manage. You cope.

Intolerable means the cup has overflowed. There is simply no more room. The thing in question is too much.

This is why the word carries a strong sense of urgency or crisis. When something is intolerable, the unspoken message is: "This cannot continue. Something must change."

The word is flexible and can describe many types of experiences:

Physical suffering

The pain from the injury was intolerable — she had to be rushed to the hospital.

Here, the pain is so intense that no one could reasonably be expected to just "handle it."

Emotional or psychological distress

Living under constant criticism from his boss became intolerable, and he finally resigned.

The suffering here is mental. The situation has worn a person down to the point of no return.

Behavior

His rudeness at the dinner table was intolerable.

Here, someone's actions are so disrespectful or offensive that they cross a clear line of what is acceptable.

Conditions or environments

The heat inside the factory was intolerable — workers could barely breathe.

The physical environment is so extreme that functioning normally is impossible.

A situation or circumstance

The injustice being committed against those people is intolerable and must be addressed immediately.

This use often appears in serious, formal, or moral contexts — calling something intolerable is a demand for action.

It helps to see where intolerable sits on a scale of "bad":

Slightly unpleasant → Uncomfortable → Difficult → Unbearable → Intolerable

It lives near the very top of this scale. It is a strong, emphatic word. You would not normally call mild inconveniences intolerable in serious writing or speech — it would sound exaggerated. However, in casual conversation, people sometimes use it for comic effect or for emphasis ("This traffic is absolutely intolerable!"), and that is perfectly normal too.
A Key Nuance: Objectivity vs. Subjectivity

Sometimes, intolerable is used objectively — meaning most reasonable people would agree that something is unacceptable:

Slavery is an intolerable violation of human rights.

Other times, it is personal and subjective — meaning you specifically cannot endure it, even if others might manage:

I find the smell of strong perfume intolerable.

Both uses are correct. The context tells you which one is meant.

Certain words pair with intolerable very naturally. Knowing these combinations (called collocations) will help you use the word fluently:

  • Become intolerable — the situation has gradually worsened until it crossed the line
  • Find something intolerable — a personal reaction; something is too much for you
  • Utterly / absolutely / simply intolerable — intensifiers that add emphasis
  • Intolerable pain / suffering / conditions / behavior / situation — the most common nouns it describes
  • Render something intolerable — to make something reach the point of being unbearable
  • Intolerable burden — a responsibility or weight that is too heavy to carry

These words overlap with intolerable, though each has a slightly different flavor:

Unbearable — very close in meaning; often used for emotional or physical pain that feels impossible to endure. Slightly more personal and emotional in tone than intolerable.

Insufferable — most commonly used to describe a person or their behavior; someone who is arrogant, annoying, or obnoxious to an extreme degree. You would rarely call physical pain "insufferable."

Unendurable — similar to unbearable; emphasizes the impossibility of lasting through something. Slightly more formal.

Unacceptable — not as strong as intolerable; something that simply should not be permitted, but does not necessarily cause intense suffering.

The key difference: intolerable tends to carry both the idea of extreme severity and the impossibility of continuing to endure it. It is stronger than "unacceptable" and more versatile than "insufferable."

The direct antonym of intolerable is tolerable, meaning something that is just about bearable — not good, but manageable.

Other antonyms include: bearable, endurable, acceptable, pleasant.

Intolerable is used comfortably in both formal and everyday language.

In formal contexts — law, politics, ethics, journalism — it is a powerful word that calls for urgent action:

The committee declared the prison conditions intolerable and demanded immediate reform.

In everyday speech, it is used more freely and sometimes with mild exaggeration:

"This queue has been going on for an hour. It's absolutely intolerable!"
One-Line Summary to Remember It By

Intolerable = so bad, painful, or wrong that it cannot — and should not — be endured any longer.

Whenever you see or hear this word, it is signaling that a limit has been exceeded, and that something demands change, relief, or action.
9161:
Intolerance means the unwillingness to accept, respect, or put up with something or someone that is different from what you consider normal, correct, or acceptable.

Think of the word "tolerate." To tolerate something means to allow it to exist, even if you don't like it. Intolerance is the opposite of that — it is the refusal to allow, accept, or respect something different.

This word is used in two distinct situations in everyday life.

Meaning 1: Social & Attitudinal Intolerance

This is the most common and widely discussed use of the word. It refers to a person's or a group's refusal to respect or accept people who are different from them — whether that difference is in religion, race, culture, opinion, lifestyle, or identity.

Think of it this way: Imagine someone who believes that only their religion is right and that everyone who follows a different religion is wrong, evil, or inferior. They don't just privately disagree — they actively reject, disrespect, or mistreat people of other faiths. That attitude and behavior is religious intolerance.

The same logic applies across many areas:

  • Racial intolerance — rejecting or mistreating people because of their race or ethnicity.
  • Political intolerance — refusing to accept that people with different political views have any right to hold or express those views.
  • Cultural intolerance — dismissing or disrespecting the customs, traditions, or ways of life of other cultures.

Important nuance: Intolerance is not just a feeling you keep private. It usually shows itself through actions — discrimination, hostility, exclusion, or even violence. This is what makes it a serious social problem.

Example sentences:

  • "The rise in hate crimes was seen as a sign of growing racial intolerance in the country."
  • "His intolerance toward people with different opinions made it impossible to have a healthy debate."
  • "The organization was founded to fight religious intolerance and promote peaceful coexistence."

Meaning 2: Medical / Physical Intolerance

In medicine and biology, intolerance has a completely different but equally precise meaning. Here, it refers to the body's inability to handle or process a particular substance without experiencing a negative reaction.

This is not about attitude or choice — it is a physical condition. The person's body simply cannot deal with that substance properly.

The most famous example is lactose intolerance — a condition where a person's digestive system cannot properly break down lactose, which is the natural sugar found in milk and dairy products. When such a person consumes dairy, they experience symptoms like bloating, stomach cramps, or diarrhea.

Other examples:

  • Gluten intolerance — the body reacts badly to gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye.
  • Drug intolerance — a patient experiences unpleasant side effects from a medication that most people handle without trouble.
  • Glucose intolerance — the body struggles to manage blood sugar levels effectively.

Example sentences:

  • "She was diagnosed with lactose intolerance, so she switched to almond milk."
  • "His gluten intolerance meant he had to be very careful about what he ate at restaurants."
  • "The doctor noted the patient's intolerance to the antibiotic and prescribed an alternative."
The Difference Between the Two Meanings — At a Glance

In Meaning 1, intolerance is a choice — it is a mindset and a way of treating others. A person decides (consciously or not) not to accept others who are different.

In Meaning 2, intolerance is not a choice — it is a biological reality. The body has a limitation, and the person cannot simply decide to "be more tolerant" of that substance.

The context of the sentence will always make it clear which meaning is being used.

Intolerance is considered a strong, serious, and negative word in the social sense. It is not a mild word. When you call something or someone "intolerant," you are making a weighty statement. It implies:

  • A closed mind
  • An unwillingness to coexist with difference
  • Often, an element of prejudice or superiority

It is stronger than simply saying someone "disagrees" with something. Disagreement is normal and healthy. Intolerance goes further — it involves rejection, contempt, or hostility toward those who are different.

Understanding these connected words will deepen your grasp of intolerance:

  • Intolerant (adjective) — This is the describing form. "He is intolerant of other religions." A person who shows intolerance is called intolerant.
  • Tolerance (noun) — The direct opposite. It means the willingness to accept and respect differences. "The school promoted a culture of tolerance."
  • Tolerant (adjective) — The opposite of intolerant. "She was tolerant of views she personally disagreed with."
  • Bigotry (noun) — A word that is very closely related to social intolerance, and often even stronger. Bigotry specifically means extreme intolerance toward people of a different group, based on prejudice. You could say bigotry is a particularly intense or hateful form of intolerance.

ContextWhat "Intolerance" Means
Social/GeneralRefusal to accept or respect people or ideas that are different
Medical/BiologicalThe body's inability to handle a certain substance

The word "intolerance" always carries the idea of something — either a mind or a body — that cannot or will not accommodate something different or foreign to it. Whether it is a person refusing to respect another's beliefs, or a stomach unable to digest dairy, the root idea is the same: a failure or refusal to handle what is different.
9162:
Intolerant means unwilling or unable to accept something that is different from what you believe, prefer, or are used to.

The easiest way to feel the difference between tolerant and intolerant is this:

A tolerant person says: "I don't agree with you, but I accept that you have the right to think or be that way."

An intolerant person says: "I cannot — or will not — accept that you think or are that way."

Tolerance is the ability to make space for difference. Intolerance is the refusal to make that space.
The three main ways it is used

1. Social and personal attitudes (the most important sense)

This is the most significant and widely used sense of the word. When someone is described as intolerant of a group of people, a religion, a lifestyle, or a set of beliefs, it means they refuse to accept, respect, or peacefully coexist with those people or beliefs. They react with hostility, dismissal, or rejection toward whatever is different from themselves.

Examples:

  • "He is intolerant of people who practice a different religion." — He refuses to accept or respect those who worship differently from him.
  • "The government was intolerant of any political opposition." — It refused to allow dissent to exist at all.
  • "She is deeply intolerant of lifestyles she doesn't understand." — She reacts with hostility to people who live differently from her.

This kind of intolerance sits close to bigotry (a strong, unreasonable dislike of people who are different), narrow-mindedness (refusing to consider other perspectives), and prejudice (judging people negatively without fair reason).

A very important point here: being intolerant is not the same as simply disagreeing. You can disagree with someone's views wholeheartedly and still be tolerant — as long as you accept their right to hold those views. Intolerance goes further. It means you refuse to allow that difference to exist alongside you. It is not just a private feeling; it is an active, rejecting attitude.

2. Everyday behavior and personality

On a less severe level, someone can be intolerant in the sense of having very little patience for something — finding it extremely difficult to put up with, even when it's a small or everyday thing.

Examples:

  • "She is intolerant of rudeness." — Even mild rudeness upsets her deeply; she cannot brush it off.
  • "He is intolerant of noise." — Small sounds bother him greatly; he cannot concentrate or stay calm around them.
  • "My manager is intolerant of delays." — She reacts very strongly to anything that runs late; she has zero patience for it.

In this everyday sense, intolerant is close in meaning to "easily bothered," "impatient," or "having a very low threshold for." It doesn't always carry a moral judgement — it might simply describe someone's temperament or sensitivity toward a particular thing.

3. The medical and biological sense

When a person's body is intolerant of a substance, it means the body cannot properly process or handle that substance — it reacts with symptoms like pain, discomfort, or illness.

Examples:

  • "She is lactose intolerant." — Her body cannot properly digest lactose (the natural sugar found in milk and dairy products), so consuming them makes her unwell.
  • "He is gluten intolerant." — His body reacts badly to gluten (a protein found in wheat and several grains).
  • "She was found to be intolerant to a certain antibiotic." — Her body responds poorly to that medicine.

In this medical sense, the word has nothing to do with attitude or feelings. It is purely about the body's physical inability to process something without a harmful reaction. This is why a doctor might say someone is "intolerant to" a drug or food — they don't mean the person dislikes it, they mean the body rejects it.
The word it pairs with: "of" or "toward"

In all its senses, intolerant almost always comes with the preposition of — and sometimes toward:

  • intolerant of different beliefs
  • intolerant of criticism
  • intolerant toward minority groups
  • intolerant of lactose

This is the natural, correct way to use it in a sentence.

Intolerant is not a black-and-white word — it covers a wide spectrum of intensity.

Someone can be slightly intolerant of something (a little impatient, easily irritated) all the way to deeply or profoundly intolerant (holding strong, active prejudice against a group of people). The same word is used, but the context tells you how serious the intolerance is. Pay attention to words around it: "slightly," "somewhat," "deeply," "fiercely," and "completely" are all common companions that signal how intense the intolerance is.
The direct opposite of intolerant is tolerant — willing to accept, respect, or put up with something that is different from what you believe or prefer, even if you don't like or agree with it.

Intolerance (noun) — the quality or state of being intolerant.
"His intolerance of other cultures made him very difficult to work with."

Intolerantly (adverb) — in an intolerant manner.
"She reacted intolerantly to his suggestion."

Tolerate (verb) — to accept or endure something you may not like.
"He simply could not tolerate the noise."

Intolerable (adjective) — note that this is a different word. It doesn't describe a person's attitude — it describes something that is too bad or painful to be endured. "The heat was intolerable" means the heat was unbearably bad. Do not confuse these two.

Intolerant, in its adjective form, means unwilling or unable to accept something that differs from what one believes, prefers, or is accustomed to. Its most powerful use is social — describing someone who refuses to accept that other people can hold different beliefs, identities, or ways of living. In a softer sense, it describes a person who has very little patience for something that bothers them. And in medicine, it describes a body that cannot handle a particular substance without reacting negatively. In all cases, the word points to a failure to accommodate difference — whether that failure is moral, psychological, or purely physical.
9163:
When you speak, your voice doesn't stay at one flat, unchanging pitch the whole time. It rises and falls as you talk — like gentle hills and valleys. Intonation is the name for this rising and falling pattern of your speaking voice.

Think of intonation as the music of speech. Even if you listen to someone speak a language you've never heard before, you can often sense whether they're asking a question, making a firm statement, or expressing surprise. That sense you get comes entirely from intonation.

Intonation isn't just decoration. It carries real meaning and does several important jobs in communication.

It separates questions from statements. Take the exact same words: "You're coming tonight." If your voice falls at the end, it's a statement — you're telling someone something. If your voice rises at the end, it becomes a question — you're asking. The words are completely identical. The only thing that changes is intonation.

It expresses feelings and attitude. Your words might say "Oh, that's great," but a warm, rising-then-falling tone means you genuinely mean it, while a flat, barely-moving tone suggests boredom or sarcasm. Intonation reveals the emotion behind your words, often more honestly than the words themselves.

It signals whether you've finished speaking. When your voice drops sharply at the end of a sentence, it tells the other person: "I'm done — your turn." When your voice stays level or rises, it signals: "I'm not finished yet, keep listening." This is how conversations flow so naturally without people constantly interrupting each other.

It highlights what matters most. By using a particular intonation pattern on a specific word, a speaker points to the key part of a sentence. Consider: "I didn't steal the book" (I just borrowed it) versus "I didn't steal the book" (I stole something else). The words are the same, but the intonation puts a spotlight on different words, changing the entire message.

There are four core intonation patterns in English.

Falling intonation is when your voice slides downward at the end. This is the most common pattern, used for plain statements ("The train leaves at noon"), commands ("Close the door"), and questions beginning with words like who, what, where, when, why, or how ("Where did you go?").

Rising intonation is when your voice climbs upward at the end. It's used for yes/no questions ("Did you eat?"), polite requests, and situations where you're uncertain. It also appears in lists — your voice rises on each item except the last, where it falls to signal the list is complete. "I bought apples, oranges, and bananas." — the final word falls, telling the listener: "That's all."

Fall-rise intonation is when your voice first dips down and then curves back up. This pattern is used to hint at something left unsaid, to express mild doubt, or to disagree politely. When someone says "I suppose it could work..." with a fall-rise, they're really signalling uncertainty — something like "but I'm not fully convinced."

Rise-fall intonation is when your voice rises and then drops steeply. This conveys strong feeling, great certainty, or being very definitive. "Of course I'll help you!" said with a rise-fall carries warmth and emphasis that a flat delivery simply cannot.

The word carries a second meaning in the world of music. Here, intonation refers to how accurately a musician or singer produces the correct pitch — whether they are in tune or not. A violinist praised for good intonation is one whose notes land at exactly the right frequencies, neither a little too high (sharp) nor a little too low (flat). Poor intonation in music is that slightly-off, uncomfortable sound that signals a note hasn't landed where it should.

In religious and choral traditions — such as Gregorian chant — intonation refers specifically to the short opening phrase sung alone by a single voice (a priest or a cantor) before the full choir joins in. This solo opening is the intonation: it sets the pitch and gets everyone aligned before the group begins singing together.

Intonation in speech is about how you say something, not just what you say. Two sentences built from the exact same words can carry entirely different meanings, emotions, and intentions based on intonation alone. It is one of the most powerful tools in human communication — and one of the most unconscious, because native speakers use it without ever thinking about it.

For language learners, actors, public speakers, teachers, and singers, understanding intonation consciously is a transformative skill. It's the difference between words that land flatly and words that truly connect.
9164: To intone something means to say or speak it in a slow, steady, and deliberately controlled voice — one that is measured, solemn, and often faintly musical or chant-like. It sits somewhere between speaking and singing. The voice doesn't jump around emotionally; instead, it holds an even, sustained tone throughout, moving at a careful, unhurried pace.
The quality of voice it describes

This is the heart of the word. When someone intones, their voice sounds deliberate and formal — like each word is being delivered with intention and weight. Imagine a monk reciting a prayer in a low, even voice, stretching each syllable slightly. Or a judge slowly reading a verdict aloud, giving every word equal, grave importance. That controlled, ceremonial, almost ritualistic quality of speaking — that is intoning. The voice is not flat in a dead way; it is flat in a purposeful, composed way.

This is where "intone" is most at home. Priests, monks, cantors, and religious leaders intone prayers, psalms, and responses during services. The word captures how these figures don't simply read or speak — they deliver sacred words in a voice that feels like a performance of reverence. "The priest intoned the opening prayer as the congregation bowed their heads." In music, particularly in choral and liturgical traditions, a cantor will intone the opening note or phrase of a hymn or plainchant — meaning they sing the beginning alone before others join in.

Beyond religion, "intone" suits any setting where someone speaks with deliberate gravity and formality. "The headmistress intoned the school's founding values at the ceremony." The word suggests that the speaker sees the moment as important, worthy of a controlled, solemn delivery. It gives the act of speaking a ceremonial quality.
When it carries a slightly negative shade

"Intone" can also be used with a gentle ironic or critical edge. If a writer says a character "intoned" their words, they might be quietly suggesting the person's voice was droning, monotonous, or overly pompous — that the speaker was being unnecessarily stiff or robotic. "He intoned the company policy for the fourth time, putting half the room to sleep." The word doesn't always mean this, but context can push it in this direction. So "intone" can sometimes wink at the audience: this person thinks what they're saying is very important, perhaps more than it is.
How it differs from similar words

To chant is very close to intoning, but chanting is more clearly musical and repetitive — you chant the same phrase over and over in a rhythm. Intoning can be a one-time, non-repetitive delivery. To recite means to say something from memory, and the focus is on the content being memorized — not on the quality of the voice. To drone specifically means speaking in a dull, monotonous way that bores people — it is almost always negative. Intoning, by contrast, can be solemn and dignified. And plain saying or speaking is neutral — it tells you nothing about how the voice sounds. "Intone" always tells you something about the character and quality of the voice itself.

Use "intone" when someone speaks in a slow, even, controlled, solemn voice — one that feels deliberate and ceremonial, whether in a church, a courtroom, a formal ceremony, or even (with a touch of irony) in everyday life when someone is being overly grave or monotonous. The word always points to how something is said, not just what is said.
9165:
To intoxicate someone means to cause them to lose their normal control — over their body, their mind, or their emotions — usually as a result of a powerful substance or an overwhelming feeling.

Think of it this way: your mind and body have a normal, steady state — you think clearly, move normally, and feel balanced. When something intoxicates you, it disrupts that steady state and pulls you away from your normal self.

This word works in two closely connected ways:

1. The Physical Meaning (Literal)

When a substance — most commonly alcohol or drugs — enters your body and affects your brain so strongly that you lose clear thinking, steady movement, or proper judgment, that substance intoxicates you.

Drinking five glasses of whiskey quickly will intoxicate almost anyone.

The fumes from the chemical were strong enough to intoxicate the workers in the room.

Here, to intoxicate means the substance is actively poisoning or overwhelming the brain's normal functioning. This is why a person who has drunk too much speaks in a slurred way, stumbles when walking, makes poor decisions, and cannot think straight — they have been intoxicated.

Notice that the substance does the intoxicating. Alcohol intoxicates the person. The person doesn't do it to themselves voluntarily — it happens to them as a result of what they consumed.

Key point: The word does not only mean "drunk." It covers any substance that disrupts the brain — alcohol, drugs, certain poisons, even toxic fumes. However, in everyday speech, it is most commonly used in relation to alcohol.

2. The Emotional/Figurative Meaning

This is a very powerful and widely used meaning. Something can intoxicate you not through chemicals, but through sheer emotional force — so much so that you feel the same kind of dizziness, loss of self-control, and overwhelming pleasure that a physical substance causes.

The applause and adoration of the crowd intoxicated her — she forgot all her nerves and exhaustion.

The beauty of the mountain landscape intoxicated him; he stood there speechless for a long time.

Power intoxicated the young king, and he stopped listening to wise advice.

Here, the word is used to describe a feeling so intense that it takes over your normal rational mind, just like alcohol does. You are so swept up in joy, beauty, excitement, love, or power that you lose your usual clear-headedness.

This figurative use carries a slightly dangerous edge to it — a hint that the feeling, beautiful as it may be, is overwhelming and possibly clouds your judgment. It's stronger than just saying something "excited" you or "pleased" you. It means you were completely overtaken by it.
How the Word Changes Form (And Still Means the Same Thing)

Understanding these forms will help you recognize the word in different sentences:

  • Intoxicates — present tense, used with he/she/it.

    "Fame intoxicates people who aren't prepared for it."

  • Intoxicated — past tense, or used as an adjective to describe a person's state.

    "He was clearly intoxicated and could not drive."
    "An intoxicated person should not make important decisions."

  • Intoxicating — used as an adjective to describe the thing that causes the effect. If something is intoxicating, it has the power to intoxicate.

    "The perfume had an intoxicating scent." (so beautiful and strong it almost makes you dizzy)
    "There is something intoxicating about performing on stage."

This is not a mild word. It implies a strong, powerful, overwhelming effect. Compare:

  • "The wine relaxed him." → mild effect, he's still himself.
  • "The wine intoxicated him." → strong effect, he's no longer fully in control.

Similarly in the figurative sense:

  • "The music pleased her." → she enjoyed it.
  • "The music intoxicated her." → she was completely swept away by it, lost in it.

So whenever you use or read this word, understand that something powerful is at work — something that takes over.
One Sentence to Tie It All Together

To intoxicate is to overpower someone's normal state of mind — whether through a substance that enters the body, or through an experience so intense it feels the same way — leaving them unable to think, feel, or behave as they normally would.
9166: Intoxicated describes a state where something has entered a person's body or mind and significantly altered the way they think, feel, or behave — to the point where they are no longer fully in control of themselves.

Most of the time, when people say someone is intoxicated, they mean that person has consumed alcohol or drugs, and those substances have affected their brain and body noticeably.

Think of it this way: you drink a small amount of alcohol and feel a little relaxed. That's mild. But if you keep drinking, a point comes where your words start to slur, your balance becomes shaky, your judgment weakens, and your reactions slow down. That is the state of being intoxicated.

Key things that characterize this state:

  • The brain's normal functioning is disrupted by a substance.
  • The person has reduced control over their thoughts, speech, and movement.
  • Their judgment and decision-making become poor.
  • They may feel unusually happy, sleepy, aggressive, or confused — depending on the substance.

Examples:

  • "The driver was arrested because he was intoxicated."
  • "She was so intoxicated that she could barely stand up."
  • "The doctor noted that the patient appeared intoxicated upon arrival."

Notice that "intoxicated" is often used in formal, legal, or medical contexts. A police officer, a judge, or a doctor is more likely to say "intoxicated" rather than "drunk." In everyday conversation, people more commonly say drunk, wasted, high, or buzzed — but "intoxicated" is the precise, formal word.

"Intoxicated" doesn't always mean completely out of control. It can describe a range of severity:

  • Mildly intoxicated → slightly affected; a little slower, a little more relaxed.
  • Heavily/severely intoxicated → very strongly affected; can't think clearly, can't walk straight.

So when you see or hear the word, pay attention to the words around it (like slightly, heavily, visibly) to understand how strong the effect is.

"Intoxicated" is also used in a non-literal, poetic, or emotional sense — and this is where the word becomes truly rich.

When someone is described as intoxicated by joy, love, beauty, power, or success, it means that emotion or experience has taken such a powerful hold over them that they feel almost the same way a substance would make them feel: overwhelmed, swept away, not quite in full control of themselves — but in a good, thrilling way.

Examples:

  • "He was intoxicated by her beauty." → He was so overwhelmed by how beautiful she was that he could barely think straight.
  • "The crowd was intoxicated by the music." → The music had such a powerful effect on the crowd that they were swept up in sheer excitement.
  • "She was intoxicated with the feeling of success." → The feeling of winning was so intense it almost went to her head.

This figurative use is very common in literature, poetry, and expressive writing. It gives the idea that some experiences are so powerful they affect us like a drug — thrilling and overwhelming.

Both are correct, and you'll see them used interchangeably. There's no strong rule here:

  • Intoxicated by alcohol / love / power
  • Intoxicated with excitement / joy / success

In the literal sense (substances), "by" is slightly more common. In the figurative sense (emotions), both are widely used.

1. It doesn't always mean drunk on alcohol.
It can refer to any substance — drugs, medications, or even toxins. If someone accidentally breathes in a dangerous chemical and starts feeling dizzy and confused, they can also be described as intoxicated.

2. It is not the same as "unconscious" or "passed out."
Intoxicated means affected and impaired — the person is still awake and somewhat functional (or barely so), but not fully in control. If they have completely lost consciousness, you'd say they "passed out" — not simply that they're intoxicated.

3. It does not carry permanent meaning.
Intoxicated describes a temporary state. Once the substance leaves the body, the person is no longer intoxicated. It says nothing about a person's long-term habits or character — just their condition at a specific moment.

Knowing the other forms of this word will help you recognize and use it more flexibly:

  • Intoxicate (verb) → "Alcohol can intoxicate a person quickly."
  • Intoxicating (adjective) → describes the thing causing the effect: "an intoxicating smell," "an intoxicating experience."
  • Intoxication (noun) → the state itself: "He was charged with public intoxication."
  • Intoxicant (noun) → the substance causing the state: "Alcohol is a common intoxicant."

LiteralYour mind and body are significantly impaired by a substance (alcohol, drugs).
FigurativeYou are powerfully and overwhelmingly affected by an emotion or experience.
ToneFormal and precise — preferred in legal, medical, and literary contexts.
Key ideaLoss of full control, caused by something external acting on you.
9167: Something intoxicating is so powerfully pleasurable, exciting, or stimulating that it overwhelms your senses and pulls you in completely — almost the way alcohol affects a person who is drunk. It sweeps you away. It clouds your normal, careful thinking. It makes you want more and more of it.

The literal sense (less common in everyday use):

A substance — alcohol, a drug, a chemical — that directly impairs your brain, your coordination, and your judgment is described as intoxicating. Alcohol is the most obvious example. It enters your body, affects your brain, and causes you to lose your sharpness and control. That process, and anything that causes it, is "intoxicating" in the literal sense.

The figurative sense (the far more common use):

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in real life. When we call something intoxicating in this sense, we mean it produces a feeling so strong, so thrilling, and so overwhelming that it mimics being drunk — even though no substance is involved. You feel dizzy with excitement or pleasure. You feel swept away. You lose a little of your usual careful, level-headed self. And you desperately want to keep experiencing the feeling.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

"Intoxicating" does not simply mean nice, enjoyable, or pleasant. It means overwhelmingly good — so good that it almost takes away your ability to think straight. The feeling borders on being too much to handle. There is always a sense of being under a powerful spell.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The music was pleasant." → mild, calm enjoyment. You are in control.
  • "The music was intoxicating." → so beautiful and powerful that you were almost lost inside it, swept away, barely aware of anything else around you.

The gap between those two sentences is the entire difference between ordinary enjoyment and something intoxicating.

The beauty of this word is how widely it can be applied — to smells, people, feelings, ideas, places, experiences.

A scent:
"The intoxicating aroma of coffee and spices hit her the moment she opened the door."
→ The smell was so powerfully wonderful that it almost stopped her in her tracks.

A feeling:
"The intoxicating sense of freedom he felt after finishing the exam made him want to run."
→ Freedom felt so overwhelmingly good it was like being drunk on happiness.

A person:
"She had an intoxicating personality — everyone in the room was drawn to her and couldn't stop listening."
→ Her presence was so magnetic and powerful that people lost their usual composure around her.

Success or power:
"Even one small taste of victory gave him an intoxicating desire to keep winning."
→ Just a tiny experience of success felt so thrilling and addictive that it overwhelmed his usual thinking.

A place or view:
"Standing at the edge of the cliff, the view of the ocean was absolutely intoxicating."
→ The view was so breathtakingly beautiful that it overwhelmed all his senses at once.

An idea:
"The intoxicating idea of starting her own business made her forget all her fears."
→ The idea was so exciting and all-consuming that it overpowered her normal caution.
The Hidden Edge in the Word

Here is something subtle but very important. When you describe something as intoxicating, you are quietly suggesting that it has a slightly dangerous or addictive quality to it. Just as a drunk person might do things they would never do sober, someone under the influence of something "intoxicating" may act recklessly, make poor decisions, or lose their better judgment.

So the word carries two feelings at once: something wonderful, and something that removes your control. It is thrilling, but not entirely safe. That combination — pleasure + a loss of control — is the soul of the word.
Where It Sits on the Scale of Intensity

"Intoxicating" lives at the very top end of the intensity scale. Here is how it compares to similar words, from weaker to stronger:

  • Enjoyable → pleasant and mild; you are completely in control
  • Exciting → your attention is grabbed; you feel engaged and alert
  • Thrilling → your heart races; strong emotion takes over
  • Intoxicating → so overwhelming it actually affects your clarity of mind; you feel almost drunk with the experience
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close cousins of "intoxicating," but each has its own flavour:

Exhilarating focuses on energy and aliveness — a rush that makes you feel very awake and free. It does not carry as much of the "losing control" quality that "intoxicating" does. You can be exhilarated and still think clearly.

Bewitching suggests a magical, almost fairy-tale attraction. It is mostly used to describe a person's charm or beauty — the idea that they have cast a spell on you. It is softer and more mystical than "intoxicating."

Mesmerizing means you are completely unable to look away or think of anything else. It focuses on capturing total attention — like being frozen in place — more than on overwhelming pleasure.

Heady is the closest synonym and is quite interchangeable with "intoxicating." It suggests dizziness and light-headedness from excitement or strong sensation. ("A heady mix of perfumes filled the room.")

None of these quite capture what makes "intoxicating" unique: the specific combination of overwhelming pleasure + a loss of rational control + an addictive pull toward more.

The most fitting antonym is sobering — meaning something that brings you sharply back to clear-headed, cold reality. Notice how sobering comes from the same world of alcohol metaphors, which shows how deeply the word "intoxicating" is rooted in that feeling of being drunk.

Other antonyms: dull, numbing, deadening.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Intoxicating" is a slightly elevated, literary word. You are more likely to read it in a novel, a travel piece, a poem, a film review, or a food and wine article than hear it in casual everyday conversation. When a writer or speaker chooses this word, they are deliberately signalling that what they are describing is extraordinary — not just good, but breathtakingly, overwhelmingly so.

Using this word in speech lends a slightly dramatic or poetic quality to what you are saying. It is a considered, expressive choice.
The One Image That Locks It All In

Imagine drinking something so wonderful that your head spins slightly, a smile spreads across your face without you choosing to smile, you forget where you are for a moment, and all you want is one more sip. That dizzy, completely consumed, swept-away feeling — applied to anything in the world, not just a drink — is precisely what "intoxicating" means.

Intoxication means the state of having a toxic or mind-altering substance inside your body that is affecting how you think, feel, move, or behave. Think of it as your body and mind being "taken over" or "disrupted" by something you consumed or were exposed to.

The substance doing the disrupting is called an intoxicant.

This word is used in three distinct ways, and knowing all three makes you truly fluent with it.

1. The Everyday Meaning — Being Drunk

This is the most common use. When most people say "intoxication," they mean the state of being drunk from alcohol. Alcohol travels into your blood, reaches your brain, and starts changing how it works. Your speech may slur, your balance may wobble, your judgment weakens, and your reactions slow down. That whole condition — that state of being under alcohol's influence — is called intoxication.

This is why you will often see phrases like "public intoxication" (being drunk in a public place) or "signs of intoxication" (the visible clues that someone is drunk).

The degree matters here. Intoxication is not all-or-nothing. It exists on a spectrum, from mild intoxication (feeling slightly tipsy, a little relaxed or giggly) all the way to severe intoxication (barely able to stand, passing out, or in a medically dangerous state). Even at the milder end, it still counts as intoxication.

2. The Medical/Scientific Meaning — Poisoning by Any Substance

In medicine and science, intoxication has a broader meaning. It refers to the harmful or disruptive state caused by any toxic substance entering the body — not just alcohol. This includes:

  • Drugs (prescription medications taken in excess, illegal drugs, etc.)
  • Chemicals (such as carbon monoxide, lead, or pesticides)
  • Poisons (such as venom from a snake bite, or a toxic plant consumed accidentally)

So a doctor might say a patient is suffering from "opioid intoxication" (from too many painkillers) or "carbon monoxide intoxication" (from breathing in toxic gas). In this sense, intoxication is essentially another word for a state of poisoning — where a substance is doing damage or causing serious disruption to the body's normal functioning.

This is the medically precise, clinical use of the word.

3. The Figurative Meaning — Overwhelming Excitement or Pleasure

Here, no substance is involved at all. Intoxication is used metaphorically to describe a powerful, almost overwhelming feeling of excitement, joy, pleasure, or euphoria triggered by an experience or emotion. The idea is that the feeling is so strong it affects you the same way a substance would — it clouds your clear thinking, fills you with intense sensation, and makes you feel "carried away."

Common examples:

  • "The intoxication of first love" — the dizzy, all-consuming feeling of falling in love for the first time.
  • "The intoxication of power" — the addictive, heady rush that comes from being in control or having authority.
  • "The intoxication of fame" — being so caught up in celebrity and admiration that your judgment suffers.

When used this way, intoxication always implies that the feeling is strong enough to impair your judgment or sense of reality, even if just a little. It is not used for mild or ordinary pleasures. You would not say "the intoxication of a good cup of tea." The word carries weight and intensity.

In law, intoxication is a specifically defined term, usually referring to alcohol or drug impairment. Courts and police use it to determine whether a person was legally impaired at the time of an incident. Many countries define legal intoxication by a specific blood alcohol concentration (BAC) threshold — if your blood alcohol is above that level, you are legally considered intoxicated, regardless of how you feel or behave. This matters in cases involving driving, criminal responsibility, and public order offences.

Since you want a complete picture, here are the closely related forms of this word:

  • Intoxicate (verb) — to cause intoxication in someone. "The fumes began to intoxicate the workers."
  • Intoxicated (adjective) — being in the state of intoxication. "She appeared intoxicated."
  • Intoxicating (adjective) — describes something that causes or feels like intoxication. "An intoxicating perfume." or "An intoxicating mix of danger and excitement."
  • Intoxicant (noun) — the substance that causes intoxication. Alcohol and certain drugs are intoxicants.
  • Intoxication (noun, your word) — the state itself.

If you had to sum it up in one sentence: intoxication is the state in which a substance — or occasionally an overwhelmingly powerful feeling — has disrupted your normal mental or physical functioning. The disruption can be mild or severe, temporary or dangerous, caused by alcohol, a drug, a chemical, or even a metaphorical "drug" like love or power.

The word always carries the idea that something from outside your normal self has taken hold of you and changed how you operate, even if just for a moment.
9169:
Intractability is the noun that describes the quality of being extremely difficult or impossible to manage, control, solve, or change — no matter how hard you try or how many different approaches you use.

Think of it this way: imagine trying to untangle a ball of wire that has been knotted for years. You try one angle, then another, then another — and nothing works. The knot just won't give. That stubborn, unyielding resistance to being solved or loosened? That is intractability.

It's not just difficult. Intractability implies a deep, persistent, almost defiant resistance — the kind that makes you feel like no solution exists, or that any solution is so far beyond reach it might as well not exist.

The word applies to two broad categories of things:

1. People

When a person displays intractability, they are stubbornly unwilling to cooperate, compromise, or change their position — regardless of logic, evidence, or persuasion. No argument moves them. No appeal works. They refuse to budge.

"The intractability of the negotiator made any peace deal impossible — he refused every compromise offered to him."

Notice: it's not that the person simply disagrees. Intractability means their resistance is total, firm, and immune to change.

2. Problems, Situations, or Conditions

When a problem or situation has intractability, it means the problem resists every attempt to fix or resolve it. Effort after effort fails. The situation persists stubbornly no matter what is done.

"The intractability of poverty in the region baffled policymakers — decades of programs had produced little change."
How It's Used Across Different Fields

The word appears in several specific fields, each with a slightly sharpened meaning:

In Medicine

Doctors use intractability to describe a disease, pain, or symptom that does not respond to treatment. Standard medicines don't help. Alternative approaches don't help either.

"The intractability of her chronic migraines meant that even the strongest medications offered no relief."

This is why you'll see phrases like intractable pain or intractable epilepsy — these are conditions that simply will not respond to the usual tools doctors have.

In Politics and Conflict

Some disputes between nations, groups, or communities go on for decades without resolution. Their intractability means they defy all diplomatic efforts, peace talks, and interventions.

"Historians have long debated the intractability of the conflict — every ceasefire broke down within months."

In Computer Science and Mathematics

Here, intractability has a precise technical meaning: it refers to a problem that cannot be solved efficiently — meaning even the fastest computers would take an impractically long time (sometimes billions of years) to find an answer as the problem grows in size.

"The intractability of the problem meant that no known algorithm could solve it within a reasonable timeframe."

This is a cornerstone idea in theoretical computer science, especially in questions about what computers fundamentally can and cannot do quickly.

Intractability is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of frustration, helplessness, and exhaustion — the feeling you get after trying everything and still failing. When someone calls a problem "intractable," they are often quietly communicating:

  • We've tried.
  • Nothing has worked.
  • This may not have a solution — at least not an easy or obvious one.

It's a word that signals defeat of effort, not just the presence of difficulty.

Not everything is equally intractable. The word exists on a spectrum:

  • A mildly intractable problem is very hard but might eventually yield to the right approach, given enough time and resources.
  • A deeply intractable problem resists all known approaches — and may be fundamentally unsolvable, at least with current understanding.

So when you see the word used, ask yourself: is the writer suggesting this is hard, or is this writer suggesting this is essentially impossible? Context will usually tell you.

Understanding how the word transforms helps you recognize it everywhere:

  • Intractable (adjective) — describes the thing that resists: "an intractable problem," "an intractable person"
  • Intractably (adverb) — describes how something resists: "intractably stubborn," "intractably complex"
  • Intractability (noun) — names the quality or state itself: "the intractability of the disease"
Intractability is the quality of being so stubbornly resistant to change, control, or solution that no amount of effort seems capable of fixing or moving it.

If you want to remember this word forever, think of it this way:

"Tract" comes from the idea of pulling or drawing something along — like a tractor pulling a plow. Now put "in-" (meaning not) in front, and add "-ability" (meaning the capacity to be). So literally: the quality of NOT being able to be pulled along — refusing to move, refusing to be managed, refusing to be solved.

That's intractability: the thing that will not be moved.
